chapterTitle: Understanding the Core Pillars of System Design
aiGenerationNote:
Design a 12-minute animated video. Visually represent each of the seven core pillars (Scalability, Reliability, Availability, Performance, Maintainability, Security, Cost) with distinct, memorable icons or short animations (e.g., scaling bars for scalability, interlocking gears for reliability, uptime clock for availability). For each pillar, provide a concise definition and a real-world example of its application or failure. Include a segment demonstrating the trade-offs between two pillars (e.g., a tug-of-war animation between "Consistency" and "Availability" with CAP theorem briefly mentioned as context). Use clear, professional narration and ensure all visual elements have appropriate alt text.

screens.title: Understanding the Core Pillars of System Design
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson we focus on the non-functional requirements that define how a system behaves, not just what it does. You will learn practical definitions and examples of six core pillars: scalability, reliability, availability, performance, maintainability, and security. We’ll show concrete techniques — like horizontal scaling, redundancy, caching, and observability — and explain the trade-offs you must weigh when designing under constraints. For example, improving consistency can cost you latency or availability; adding encryption adds processing overhead. By the end you’ll be able to prioritize pillars for a real service and justify trade-offs with clear reasoning. As you review the three highlighted topics below, think about a system you know and which pillar would break first when usage grows. That reflection will help you make design choices that balance technical reality with product needs.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.3 › Understanding the Core Pillars
Understanding the Core Pillars of System Design
A focused guide to the non-functional requirements that shape robust distributed systems and the trade-offs they demand.
In this lesson
Understand pillars, techniques, and trade-offs that drive production readiness.
Overview
Non-functional requirements define the observable qualities of a system — how it scales, how often it stays online, how fast it responds, and how easy it is to evolve and protect. They matter more as systems grow.
Consider these pillars as design constraints you review at every architecture decision.
Scalability
Grow capacity by adding resources; horizontal scaling avoids single points of failure.
Reliability
Design for correctness over time using redundancy and fault tolerance.
Availability
Keep the service reachable; measure in uptime percentages or "nines".
Explore Key Topics
Each topic below is expanded in the following lesson screens with examples and trade-offs you will need to justify in interviews.
Scalability
Vertical vs horizontal growth and common techniques like sharding and load balancing.
Performance
Latency and throughput, caching, CDNs and async patterns to reduce user-visible delay.
Security
Authentication, authorization, encryption and rate limiting to protect data and services.
Visual summary
Pillars as constraints
Treat them as design levers you tune per product goals.
Trade-offs are inevitable
Expect to trade latency for consistency or security for performance when needed.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: By the end of these screens you will be able to identify and define the key non-functional requirements that drive system behavior. First, you’ll name each pillar and provide a clear definition that distinguishes reliability from availability, and latency from throughput. Second, you will explain practical implications: how scalability techniques like horizontal sharding or load balancing enable growth, and how caching and CDNs improve perceived performance. Third, you will understand maintainability and security as long-term investments that reduce operational cost and risk. Fourth, you will recognize common trade-offs and explain why improving one pillar often affects another. For example, improving encryption or stronger consistency often increases latency. You will practice prioritizing pillars for a hypothetical product and justify those choices with concrete consequences. These skills will help you structure interview answers and architectural choices in real projects.

Module 1 › Chapter 1.3 › Learning Objectives
Learning Objectives
Four measurable skills you will demonstrate after completing this chapter.
01
Identify and define NFRs
You will name the core pillars and explain why each is a system-level quality. Verified competency milestone.
Mnemonic: Group pillars into operational, performance, and security clusters to remember purpose and techniques.
02
Explain scalability, reliability, availability
You will describe practical effects and common techniques, like load balancers, sharding, replicas and failover. Verified competency milestone.
Mnemonic: Think "grow, survive, stay online" to keep the three distinct.
03
Understand performance and maintainability
You will measure latency and throughput, and propose approaches like caching and modular design to improve them. Verified competency milestone.
Mnemonic: Performance is speed; maintainability is the long-term cost to change.
04
Recognize trade-offs and interdependencies
You will explain how prioritizing one pillar affects others and present a reasoned trade-off for a given scenario. Verified competency milestone.
Mnemonic: Picture a balance scale — tuning one side tilts others.

screens.title: Learning Objectives — Practical Skills
screens.narratorSegment: This second objectives slide focuses on practical application and judgement. You will be able to justify the choice of techniques such as horizontal scaling, replication, caching, CDNs, and asynchronous processing when asked why they are appropriate. You will also practice explaining differences like reliability versus availability with concrete metrics, such as explaining what "nines" mean for downtime. Importantly, you will learn to weigh trade-offs: for instance, how stricter data consistency can increase latency, or how aggressive caching can complicate correctness. These judgments are what interviewers look for — clear, scenario-based reasoning that ties a pillar to a technique and to measurable consequences. Practice forming brief answers that state the priority, propose one or two techniques, and acknowledge a downside. Learning Objectives — Practical Skills means build the habit of pairing a pillar with one practical technique and one measurable outcome when you explain design choices.. In practical terms, how you'll apply these pillars in architecture and interviews. A simple real-world example is helpful here, because students learn best when they can connect the idea to a familiar situation. This matters because it gives the learner a clear mental model and helps them connect the concept to later examples and problems. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Learning Objectives — Practical Skills
Practice connecting pillars to techniques and measurable effects.
Explain one technique per pillar
For every pillar be ready to name one practical approach and one metric to measure success. Example: For performance, use caching and measure latency percentiles.
Scalability

Practice structure for interview answers

screens.title: Non-functional Requirements (NFRs)
screens.narratorSegment: Non-functional requirements, or NFRs, are the quality attributes that describe how a system performs and operates instead of what functions it provides. They include measures like uptime, response time, and the ability to scale. Treating NFRs as first-class concerns means designing components, operations, and testing practices to meet them. For instance, a feature that works functionally but cannot handle growth is not production-ready. Concrete example: imagine a social feed that returns posts correctly but takes five seconds per request under moderate load. The behavior is correct, but latency and throughput NFRs fail and users will abandon it. A common misconception is confusing NFRs with functional requirements — they are orthogonal: NFRs constrain how features should behave under load, failure, and change. Key practices include defining measurable targets (SLOs), instrumenting observability, and building components that can be independently scaled or replaced. Takeaway: always quantify an NFR before choosing a technique, and include expected metrics in any architecture justification. Which measurable target would you pick first for a read-heavy A P I? Non-functional Requirements (NFRs) means nfrs describe system qualities and must be measurable; they guide design choices and trade-offs.. In practical terms, what nfrs are and why they matter for architecture. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.3 › NFRs
Non-functional Requirements (NFRs)
Quality attributes that guide architecture and operations.
Definition
NFRs define how well a system performs under specific conditions. They include scalability, reliability, availability, performance, maintainability, and security. Each should be tied to measurable targets or service-level objectives.
Example
A feed API that is functionally correct but responds in five seconds under moderate load fails performance NFRs and drives users away.
Common mistake
Confusing NFRs with features. NFRs are constraints on behavior, not capabilities to add.
Key Takeaway

Define measurable SLOs for each NFR before choosing architecture techniques; instrument to verify them.

Teaching visual — Pillar cards
Scalability
Add capacity to handle growth without failing targets.
Reliability
Probability of correct operation over time; achieved with redundancy.
Availability
Percentage of time the system is reachable; measured in "nines".
Performance
Latency and throughput metrics that determine user experience.
Question: Which single measurable target would you set first for your product and why?

screens.title: Scalability: Vertical vs Horizontal
screens.narratorSegment: Scalability is the system’s ability to handle increasing load by adding resources. There are two common approaches: vertical scaling, which increases resources on a single machine, and horizontal scaling, which adds more machines or instances. Vertical scaling is simple and often the fastest short-term fix: add C P U, memory, or disk. But it hits physical limits and tends to create a single point of failure. Horizontal scaling is more complex: you partition work across multiple nodes, use load balancers to distribute traffic, shard data so each node owns a subset, and use distributed caches to reduce load on origin stores. A concrete example: a web application that starts with one database server and moves to replicated read replicas and then shards write traffic into multiple database partitions as write load grows. A common misconception is postponing horizontal scaling until "we need it"—that can lead to expensive re-architecture. Plan for horizontal patterns early where elasticity is expected. Key takeaway: pick vertical scaling for small growth and simple setups, and design for horizontal scaling when you expect rapid variability or high sustained scale.

keyIdea.title: Scalability tip
keyIdea.text: Start with simple scaling but design boundaries so you can switch to horizontal techniques without a full rewrite.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.3 › Scalability
Scalability: Vertical vs Horizontal
When and how to grow system capacity.
Process: scaling progression
1
Vertical scale (simple)
Add CPU, memory, or disk. Use for initial growth but expect capacity limits and single point of failure.
2
Horizontal scale (distributed)
Add instances, use load balancers, shard data, and introduce replication for fault tolerance and elasticity.
3
Operational techniques
Automated provisioning, health checks, and capacity planning help you scale safely and predictably.
Key Takeaway

Design clear service boundaries and add observability so that scaling choices remain reversible and measurable.

Teaching visual — technique cards
Load balancer
Distributes traffic across instances and detects unhealthy nodes for failover.
Sharding
Partition data so each shard handles a subset of traffic or data, improving write scalability.
Distributed cache
Reduce load on central stores and improve read latency with a shared cache layer.

screens.title: Load Balancing, Sharding, and Caching
screens.narratorSegment: Three concrete patterns are essential when you scale horizontally: load balancing, sharding, and distributed caching. Load balancers distribute requests across healthy servers and can perform health checks and session routing. They are the first line of defense against traffic spikes. Sharding splits a dataset so each database instance owns a subset — a straightforward example is partitioning by user ID. Sharding increases write throughput by avoiding a single hot database, but it complicates queries across partitions. Distributed caching stores frequently requested data close to the application, lowering latency and origin load. A practical example: a read-heavy profile service can use a cache to serve profile reads in milliseconds while write operations update the backing store and invalidate cache entries. A common misconception is relying on caching to hide slow origin queries without fixing them; caches improve perceived performance but are short-term bandages if your storage is poorly designed. When explaining these techniques in interviews, pair each with a measurable outcome: e. g., load balancer reduces per-node C P U utilization by X percent, caching reduces average latency from 200 ms to 20 ms, and sharding increases write throughput linearly across shards.

keyIdea.text: Always state a measurable outcome for a technique; numbers make your trade-offs and choices credible.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.3 › Scalability Techniques
Load Balancing, Sharding, and Caching
Patterns that both scale capacity and improve experience.
Load Balancer
Distributes traffic, performs health checks, and prevents single-node overloads.
Sharding
Partition data across nodes to increase write capacity; requires careful routing and cross-shard queries.
Distributed Cache
Cache hot reads to lower latency and origin load; handle invalidation carefully for correctness.
Concrete scenario
A profile service serves 10,000 RPS. Add a load balancer to spread requests across 10 app servers, add a distributed cache to serve 80% of reads, and shard the user database by user-id to distribute writes. This combination raises throughput and lowers median latency.
Common misconception
Caching is not a substitute for fixing slow queries: cache helps while you optimize origin systems and data access patterns.
Key Takeaway

Pair each scaling technique with a measurable metric to justify its use and reveal hidden trade-offs.

screens.title: Reliability: Redundancy and Fault Tolerance
screens.narratorSegment: Reliability measures the probability that a system will perform its intended function without failure for a specified period under specified conditions. Practically, this means minimizing data loss, corruption, or incorrect processing. Achieving reliability requires redundancy — multiple copies of data or services — and fault tolerance so that remaining components maintain correct operation when parts fail. Error handling, monitoring, and graceful degradation are essential. A concrete example: a primary database with one or more replicas ensures that if the primary fails, a replica can take over with minimal data loss, provided replication is properly configured. A common misconception is that redundancy automatically equals reliability; it only does when replicas are consistent, failover is automated, and your operational runbooks ensure correct recovery. Another pitfall is relying solely on manual failover, which increases downtime risk. Key takeaway: architect for automatic recovery and test failure scenarios frequently so redundancy translates into real reliability. Reliability: Redundancy and Fault Tolerance means redundancy must be paired with automation and verification to deliver true reliability.. In practical terms, designing systems that continue to operate under component failures. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.3 › Reliability
Reliability: Redundancy and Fault Tolerance
How to ensure correct operation over time.
Definition and practices
Reliability is achieved through redundancy, automated failover, robust error handling, and frequent recovery testing. Observability helps detect problems before they cascade.
Example
Primary database with replicas and automated promotion reduces the probability of data loss when a node fails.
Common mistake
Assuming redundancy without automated recovery and monitoring delivers reliability. It often does not.
Key Takeaway

Redundancy must be operationalized and tested regularly to become meaningful reliability.

Teaching visual — reliability elements
Replication
Multiple copies of data to prevent loss.
Failover
Automatic switching to healthy instances to maintain operation.
Error handling
Graceful degradation and retries that avoid cascading failures.
Observability
Logging, monitoring, and tracing to detect and diagnose issues quickly.

screens.title: Availability vs Reliability
screens.narratorSegment: Availability measures how often a system is accessible to users, expressed as a percentage of uptime, while reliability measures the probability of correct operation over time. They are related: a system can reliably preserve data but still be unavailable during maintenance or failover windows. For example, a database with synchronous replication may be very reliable in terms of consistency, but a failover event or maintenance could make it temporarily unreachable, reducing availability. Availability is often communicated in "nines": 99.9% means roughly 8.76 hours of downtime per year; 99.999% gives only minutes of downtime yearly. Achieving higher availability requires redundant components across failure domains and automated failover, sometimes across regions. A common misconception is to assume that higher availability is always better without cost: increasing availability typically requires more redundancy, cross-region replication, and operational complexity. When discussing availability in interviews, include how failover is tested, whether data consistency is preserved during failover, and the operational cost of achieving the desired number of nines. Takeaway: choose an availability target based on user expectations and the cost of downtime, not on an abstract ideal.

keyIdea.title: Availability clarity
keyIdea.text: Availability is about reachability and uptime; reliability is about correctness. Both require different operational commitments.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.3 › Availability vs Reliability
Availability vs Reliability
A direct comparison to clear common confusion.
Availability
Measured as uptime percent. Techniques include multi-zone redundancy, automated failover, and global load balancing. Think in "nines" for SLA commitments.
Example: Achieving 99.99% availability may require cross-region replicas and traffic rerouting to avoid single-region outages.
Reliability
Measures correct operation over time. Achieved through redundancy, transactional guarantees, and robust error handling. It focuses on data integrity and correctness under failure.
Example: Synchronous replication can improve reliability but may increase latency and make failover more complex, impacting availability.
Metric
Availability: uptime %. Reliability: failure probability over time.
Trade-off
Stricter consistency improves reliability but can raise latency or reduce availability during partitions.
Question
Which would you prioritize for a billing system: availability or reliability? Why?

screens.title: Performance: Latency and Throughput
screens.narratorSegment: Performance captures how quickly a system responds and how much work it can do. Two central metrics are latency and throughput. Latency measures the time from request to response; throughput counts operations per second. Improving performance often requires practical changes: caching frequent data to reduce response time, using CDNs to serve static assets closer to users, optimizing database queries, and moving long-running work to asynchronous background processing. A concrete example: replacing a synchronous enrichment call in the request path with an asynchronous job can reduce request latency from hundreds of milliseconds to tens of milliseconds, while the enrichment completes later and updates the record. A common misconception is optimizing average latency only; percentiles matter more because tail latency affects user perception. For interviews, be ready to mention specific metrics you would track — median latency and 95th/99th percentiles — and one concrete technique to improve each metric. Takeaway: measure first, then choose the technique that most directly reduces your target metric while acknowledging trade-offs. Performance: Latency and Throughput means measure latency percentiles and throughput; optimize the request path and move heavy work off the critical path.. In practical terms, key metrics and techniques to improve user-visible speed. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.3 › Performance
Performance: Latency and Throughput
How fast and how much a system can work.
Latency
Time for a single request to complete. Track median and tail percentiles because long tails hurt user experience.
Technique: Move blocking work to background jobs; use caching and CDNs to reduce roundtrips.
Throughput
Operations per second a system can handle. Scale horizontally and tune bottlenecks to increase throughput.
Technique: Partition workloads, increase parallelism, and optimize data access patterns.
Concrete example
An enrichment call added 150 ms to request latency. By making the enrichment asynchronous and returning cached results immediately, median latency fell from 200 ms to 35 ms while throughput increased because threads were freed faster.
Key Takeaway

Measure percentiles and choose the most direct technique to reduce the metric that matters to users.

screens.title: Maintainability: Modularity and Observability
screens.narratorSegment: Maintainability is the ease with which a system can be modified, understood, and repaired. It directly affects the cost of future features, bug fixes, and operational work. Practical ways to improve maintainability include modular design so components have clear responsibilities, thorough documentation so engineers can onboard and reason about systems quickly, and strong observability — logging, metrics, and tracing — so issues can be diagnosed fast. A concrete example: splitting a monolithic service into smaller services with clear APIs can reduce the blast radius of changes and allow independent deployment cycles. A common mistake is prioritizing short-term delivery over modularity, which creates technical debt that slows future work. Good maintainability also includes consistent testing and clear runbooks for operational procedures. Takeaway: when asked to optimize for maintainability, propose modular decomposition, invest in observability, and set standards for documentation and testing to ensure long-term velocity. Maintainability: Modularity and Observability means invest early in modular boundaries and observability to reduce technical debt and keep development velocity high.. In practical terms, how design and practices reduce long-term cost and risk. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. narration.text: Maintainability is the ease with which a system can be modified, understood, and repaired. It directly affects the cost of future features, bug fixes, and operational work. screens.title: Security: Protecting Data and Services
screens.narratorSegment: Security protects systems from unauthorized access, misuse, and data loss. Core elements include authentication — confirming identity — and authorization — controlling what authenticated users can do. Data encryption in transit and at rest prevents attackers from reading sensitive information. Rate limiting and throttling mitigate abuse and denial-of-service attempts. Regular security audits, secret management, and least-privilege principles reduce attack surface. A concrete example: an A P I that requires authentication tokens and encrypts payloads reduces the chance of data exposure; adding per-account rate limits prevents abusive clients from degrading service for others. A common misconception is treating security as an optional layer added at the end of development. In reality, security must be designed in from the beginning because retrofitting controls often leaves gaps. When discussing security in interviews, describe specific protections you’d apply for a given threat model, and explain the operational practices to rotate keys and monitor suspicious activity. Takeaway: security is both architecture and operations — pair technical controls with monitoring and audits. Security: Protecting Data and Services
Controls and practices to keep systems safe.
Core controls
Authentication, authorization, encryption, rate limits, and secret management are the baseline. Each must be paired with monitoring and rotation policies.
Example: Token-based auth plus TLS reduces the risk of session hijacking and eavesdropping on data in transit.
Operational practices

Key Takeaway

screens.title: Trade-offs and Interdependencies
screens.narratorSegment: No pillar stands alone; system design is about balancing interdependent goals. A common trade-off is between consistency and availability: stronger consistency can increase latency or make a service less available during partitions. Adding encryption improves security but can reduce throughput or increase latency if not offloaded. Adding more replicas improves reliability and availability, but increases operational cost and complexity for writes. When you make a decision, explain which pillar you prioritize, the specific technique you’ll use, the measurable change you expect, and the downside you accept. A concrete scenario: a financial ledger prioritizes reliability and security over latency — the design might use synchronous replication and strict authorization checks that add latency but preserve correctness. Conversely, a public content feed might prioritize availability and performance, caching aggressively and accepting eventual consistency for certain data. A common misconception is to treat trade-offs as absolutes; instead, they are contextual. Key takeaway: always state priorities, expected metrics, and a mitigation plan for the accepted downside. Trade-offs and Interdependencies
Make trade-offs explicit and measurable.
Decision process
1) State priority pillar. 2) Choose technique(s). 3) State measurable expectation. 4) Acknowledge downside and mitigation. Apply this pattern in interviews and design documents.

Don’t assume one technique solves multiple pillars without cost. Adding replication improves reliability but complicates writes and consistency.

screens.title: Hands-on Activity: Pillar Prioritization for a Streaming Service
screens.narratorSegment: This activity asks you to prioritize the pillars for a video streaming service and justify each choice. Step one: choose the top three pillars from the list provided in the chapter. Step two: for each choice, write a short paragraph explaining why neglecting it would harm the product. fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson we focus on the non-functional requirements that define how a system behaves, not just what it does. You will learn practical definitions and examples of six core pillars: scalability, reliability, availability, performance, maintainability, and security. We’ll show concrete techniques — like horizontal scaling, redundancy, caching, and observability — and explain the trade-offs you must weigh when designing under constraints. For example, improving consistency can cost you latency or availability; adding encryption adds processing overhead. By the end you’ll be able to prioritize pillars for a real service and justify trade-offs with clear reasoning. As you review the three highlighted topics below, think about a system you know and which pillar would break first when usage grows. That reflection will help you make design choices that balance technical reality with product needs.

By the end of these screens you will be able to identify and define the key non-functional requirements that drive system behavior. First, you’ll name each pillar and provide a clear definition that distinguishes reliability from availability, and latency from throughput. Second, you will explain practical implications: how scalability techniques like horizontal sharding or load balancing enable growth, and how caching and CDNs improve perceived performance. Third, you will understand maintainability and security as long-term investments that reduce operational cost and risk. Fourth, you will recognize common trade-offs and explain why improving one pillar often affects another. For example, improving encryption or stronger consistency often increases latency. You will practice prioritizing pillars for a hypothetical product and justify those choices with concrete consequences. These skills will help you structure interview answers and architectural choices in real projects.

This second objectives slide focuses on practical application and judgement. You will be able to justify the choice of techniques such as horizontal scaling, replication, caching, CDNs, and asynchronous processing when asked why they are appropriate. You will also practice explaining differences like reliability versus availability with concrete metrics, such as explaining what "nines" mean for downtime. Importantly, you will learn to weigh trade-offs: for instance, how stricter data consistency can increase latency, or how aggressive caching can complicate correctness. These judgments are what interviewers look for — clear, scenario-based reasoning that ties a pillar to a technique and to measurable consequences. Practice forming brief answers that state the priority, propose one or two techniques, and acknowledge a downside. Learning Objectives — Practical Skills means build the habit of pairing a pillar with one practical technique and one measurable outcome when you explain design choices.. In practical terms, how you'll apply these pillars in architecture and interviews. A simple real-world example is helpful here, because students learn best when they can connect the idea to a familiar situation. This matters because it gives the learner a clear mental model and helps them connect the concept to later examples and problems. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Non-functional requirements, or NFRs, are the quality attributes that describe how a system performs and operates instead of what functions it provides. They include measures like uptime, response time, and the ability to scale. Treating NFRs as first-class concerns means designing components, operations, and testing practices to meet them. For instance, a feature that works functionally but cannot handle growth is not production-ready. Concrete example: imagine a social feed that returns posts correctly but takes five seconds per request under moderate load. The behavior is correct, but latency and throughput NFRs fail and users will abandon it. A common misconception is confusing NFRs with functional requirements — they are orthogonal: NFRs constrain how features should behave under load, failure, and change. Key practices include defining measurable targets (SLOs), instrumenting observability, and building components that can be independently scaled or replaced. Takeaway: always quantify an NFR before choosing a technique, and include expected metrics in any architecture justification. Which measurable target would you pick first for a read-heavy A P I? Non-functional Requirements (NFRs) means nfrs describe system qualities and must be measurable; they guide design choices and trade-offs.. In practical terms, what nfrs are and why they matter for architecture. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Scalability is the system’s ability to handle increasing load by adding resources. There are two common approaches: vertical scaling, which increases resources on a single machine, and horizontal scaling, which adds more machines or instances. Vertical scaling is simple and often the fastest short-term fix: add C P U, memory, or disk. But it hits physical limits and tends to create a single point of failure. Horizontal scaling is more complex: you partition work across multiple nodes, use load balancers to distribute traffic, shard data so each node owns a subset, and use distributed caches to reduce load on origin stores. A concrete example: a web application that starts with one database server and moves to replicated read replicas and then shards write traffic into multiple database partitions as write load grows. A common misconception is postponing horizontal scaling until "we need it"—that can lead to expensive re-architecture. Plan for horizontal patterns early where elasticity is expected. Key takeaway: pick vertical scaling for small growth and simple setups, and design for horizontal scaling when you expect rapid variability or high sustained scale.

Three concrete patterns are essential when you scale horizontally: load balancing, sharding, and distributed caching. Load balancers distribute requests across healthy servers and can perform health checks and session routing. They are the first line of defense against traffic spikes. Sharding splits a dataset so each database instance owns a subset — a straightforward example is partitioning by user ID. Sharding increases write throughput by avoiding a single hot database, but it complicates queries across partitions. Distributed caching stores frequently requested data close to the application, lowering latency and origin load. A practical example: a read-heavy profile service can use a cache to serve profile reads in milliseconds while write operations update the backing store and invalidate cache entries. A common misconception is relying on caching to hide slow origin queries without fixing them; caches improve perceived performance but are short-term bandages if your storage is poorly designed. When explaining these techniques in interviews, pair each with a measurable outcome: e. g., load balancer reduces per-node C P U utilization by X percent, caching reduces average latency from 200 ms to 20 ms, and sharding increases write throughput linearly across shards.

Reliability measures the probability that a system will perform its intended function without failure for a specified period under specified conditions. Practically, this means minimizing data loss, corruption, or incorrect processing. Achieving reliability requires redundancy — multiple copies of data or services — and fault tolerance so that remaining components maintain correct operation when parts fail. Error handling, monitoring, and graceful degradation are essential. A concrete example: a primary database with one or more replicas ensures that if the primary fails, a replica can take over with minimal data loss, provided replication is properly configured. A common misconception is that redundancy automatically equals reliability; it only does when replicas are consistent, failover is automated, and your operational runbooks ensure correct recovery. Another pitfall is relying solely on manual failover, which increases downtime risk. Key takeaway: architect for automatic recovery and test failure scenarios frequently so redundancy translates into real reliability. Reliability: Redundancy and Fault Tolerance means redundancy must be paired with automation and verification to deliver true reliability.. In practical terms, designing systems that continue to operate under component failures. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Availability measures how often a system is accessible to users, expressed as a percentage of uptime, while reliability measures the probability of correct operation over time. They are related: a system can reliably preserve data but still be unavailable during maintenance or failover windows. For example, a database with synchronous replication may be very reliable in terms of consistency, but a failover event or maintenance could make it temporarily unreachable, reducing availability. Availability is often communicated in "nines": 99.9% means roughly 8.76 hours of downtime per year; 99.999% gives only minutes of downtime yearly. Achieving higher availability requires redundant components across failure domains and automated failover, sometimes across regions. A common misconception is to assume that higher availability is always better without cost: increasing availability typically requires more redundancy, cross-region replication, and operational complexity. When discussing availability in interviews, include how failover is tested, whether data consistency is preserved during failover, and the operational cost of achieving the desired number of nines. Takeaway: choose an availability target based on user expectations and the cost of downtime, not on an abstract ideal.

Performance captures how quickly a system responds and how much work it can do. Two central metrics are latency and throughput. Latency measures the time from request to response; throughput counts operations per second. Improving performance often requires practical changes: caching frequent data to reduce response time, using CDNs to serve static assets closer to users, optimizing database queries, and moving long-running work to asynchronous background processing. A concrete example: replacing a synchronous enrichment call in the request path with an asynchronous job can reduce request latency from hundreds of milliseconds to tens of milliseconds, while the enrichment completes later and updates the record. A common misconception is optimizing average latency only; percentiles matter more because tail latency affects user perception. For interviews, be ready to mention specific metrics you would track — median latency and 95th/99th percentiles — and one concrete technique to improve each metric. Takeaway: measure first, then choose the technique that most directly reduces your target metric while acknowledging trade-offs.
